overview: Forwards are priced by the oldest argument in finance: buy the asset today, store it until delivery, and you have manufactured the forward yourself — so the forward can only cost spot plus the net cost of that carry, or arbitrageurs eat the difference. For currencies the carry is the interest differential (covered interest parity); for commodities it is financing plus storage minus the convenience yield of holding the physical. No expectations, no forecasts of where prices go: the forward is a statement about carrying costs, not about the future.
formula_latex: F_{FX} = S\,e^{(r_d - r_f)T} \qquad\quad F_{cmdty} = S\,e^{(r + u - y)T}

variables.name: Spot price
variables.why_it_matters: The replication anchor. A forward position's delta to spot is nearly one-for-one — the model's whole content is what to multiply spot by.

variables.name: Rate differential
variables.why_it_matters: The FX carry. Higher domestic rates push the forward above spot (forward premium) — not because anyone predicts appreciation, but because holding the low-yielding currency must be compensated.

variables.name: Storage cost
variables.why_it_matters: Commodities, unlike currencies, take up space. Tanks and silos cost money, and that cost flows straight into the fair futures price.

variables.name: Convenience yield
variables.why_it_matters: The invisible dividend of holding the physical: a refinery that never runs dry. When inventories are tight y spikes above r+u, carry turns negative, and the curve inverts into backwardation — the market paying you to hold barrels.

assumptions: The asset can be bought, stored, and sold short freely (shorting physical commodities is the shakiest of these).
Carry components (rates, storage, convenience) are constant to delivery.
No transaction costs or financing spreads; one borrowing rate for everyone.
For FX: covered interest parity holds — historically excellent, though post-2008 cross-currency basis puts measurable dents in it.
limitations: Convenience yield is not observable — in practice it is backed out of futures prices, making the commodity formula partly circular.
Cross-currency basis: real FX forwards deviate from textbook parity by a basis reflecting bank funding pressures.
Says nothing about price expectations or risk premia — deliberately, but users sometimes want exactly those.
Non-storable underlyings (electricity, weather, freight) break the replication argument entirely.
when_to_use: FX forwards and swaps points, storable-commodity futures fair value, cash-and-carry arbitrage detection, and building forward curves from spot and rates.
when_not_to_use: Non-storable commodities, forwards with embedded optionality, or any question about expected future spot prices (carry is silent about them).
industry_usage: How every FX desk quotes forward points and every commodity desk reads contango versus backwardation; the first fair-value screen for calendar spreads.
